Compute the coordinates of nodes

Source: R/layout_networks.R
layout_networks.Rd

A network has no natural position on a page. Force-directed layouts place nodes so that tied nodes are close and untied nodes are pushed apart, so that clusters appear as dense regions: Kamada-Kawai ("kk") draws graph distances as geometric distances (Kamada and Kawai 1989) , Fruchterman-Reingold ("fr") balances attraction along edges and repulsion between all nodes (Fruchterman and Reingold 1991) . layout_networks() computes such coordinates with ggraph::create_layout(), which gives access to the layouts of igraph and graphlayouts, and stores them in the node table.

For a list of networks, the coordinates of a node may jump from one window to the next, which makes the plots hard to compare. With compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE, the coordinates of window \(t-1\) are used as the starting positions of the layout of window \(t\), so that the nodes present in both windows tend to stay in the same region.

Usage

layout_networks(
  graphs,
  node_id,
  layout,
  compute_dynamic_coordinates = FALSE,
  save_coordinates = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

graphs

A tbl_graph or a list of tbl_graphs.

node_id

Character scalar, the node column with a unique identifier, used to join the coordinates.

layout

Character scalar, a layout accepted by ggraph::create_layout() (e.g. "kk", "fr", "stress").

compute_dynamic_coordinates

Logical. For a list of graphs, if TRUE, each layout starts from the coordinates of the previous window (see the details).

save_coordinates

Logical. If TRUE, the coordinates are also stored in x_{layout} and y_{layout} (e.g. x_kk, y_kk), so that they are not lost when another layout is computed.

...

Other arguments of the layout (see ggraph::create_layout() and the igraph or graphlayouts function behind it).

Value

The same object as graphs, with node columns x and y (any existing x and y are replaced) and, if save_coordinates = TRUE, x_{layout} and y_{layout}.

Details

Force-directed layouts are stochastic and sensitive to the starting positions: set a seed with set.seed() before calling the function to reproduce a figure. Distances in such plots are only roughly interpretable: two clusters drawn side by side are more tied than two clusters at opposite ends, but distances should not be measured.

Weights. igraph uses the weight edge column automatically, but not always in the same way: Fruchterman-Reingold ("fr") reads weights as attraction (heavier edges pull nodes closer), while Kamada-Kawai ("kk") reads them as distances, so that similarity weights push the most similar nodes apart and weakly tied nodes to the margins. With similarity weights, prefer "fr", or pass weights = NA to ignore them.

For dynamic coordinates, nodes absent from the previous window start at (0, 0). The starting positions are passed to the layout as its coords argument: this works only with layouts that accept it, such as "fr" and "kk" of igraph.

References

Fruchterman TMJ, Reingold EM (1991). “Graph Drawing by Force-Directed Placement.” Software: Practice and Experience, 21(11), 1129–1164. doi:10.1002/spe.4380211102 .

Kamada T, Kawai S (1989). “An Algorithm for Drawing General Undirected Graphs.” Information Processing Letters, 31(1), 7–15. doi:10.1016/0020-0190(89)90102-6 .

Examples

network <- build_network(
  nodes = subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation"),
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 2
)
set.seed(1)
network <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "fr")
head(tidygraph::as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")[c("source_id", "x", "y")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
